Let $X$ be a connected compact K\"ahler manifold of dimension $n$, let $\omega$ be a K\"ahler form, and fix a class $\alpha\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$. If $\alpha$ is nef, its classical null locus is
\[
 \operatorname{Null}(\alpha)
 =\bigcup_{\substack{V\subset X\ \mathrm{irreducible},\ \dim V>0\\
                       \int_V\alpha^{\dim V}=0}}V.
\]
The intersection number may be computed on a resolution of $V$ by pulling back a smooth closed representative. It is independent of that representative, by Stokes' theorem. For a nef and big class, the equality
\[
 E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha)=\operatorname{Null}(\alpha)
\]
is the transcendental Nakamaye theorem of Collins--Tosatti \cite{CT15Loci}. Their theorem also applies on compact manifolds in class $\mathcal C$.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:fixed-point-finite}
Let $\theta\geq0$ be smooth. Every envelope fixed point $\varphi$ satisfies
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(\varphi)
 \leq\mathbf1_{\{\varphi=0\}}\theta^n.
\]
In particular, its mass is finite, without assuming bounded mass on $X$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
We have $\varphi\leq0$. For every $j\geq0$, the envelope $P_\theta(\varphi+j,0)$ is both at least $\varphi$, since $\varphi$ is a competitor, and at most $P_\theta[\varphi]=\varphi$. Apply \cref{prop:rooftop-measure} to obtain
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(\varphi)
 \leq\mathbf1_{\{\varphi\leq-j\}}
          \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(\varphi)
      +\mathbf1_{\{\varphi=0\}}\theta^n.
\]
One must not subtract potentially infinite measures here. Instead, restrict to $\{\varphi>-t\}$ and choose $j>t$. The first term vanishes. Letting $t\to+\infty$ proves the claim by the definition of the extended measure. This is the fixed-point argument in \cite[Proposition 2.12]{ALS26}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:relative-uniform-mass-lower}
Every $u\in\mathcal E_\varphi$ admits a genuine $P_{(\varepsilon+\delta)\theta}(u)$ whenever $0<\delta<1-\varepsilon$. Consequently
\[
 \int_X\mu_u\geq(1-\varepsilon)^n v_-(\theta),
 \qquad \int_X\mu_u>0.
\]
The first bound is uniform over the class; the second is an individual assertion. Neither asserts finiteness.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Translate $u$ below $\varphi$ and use $w\in\mathcal E_0$ from \cref{lem:relative-difference-envelope}. The potential
\[
 P_{\varepsilon\theta}(\varphi)+\delta P_\theta(w/\delta)
 \leq\varphi+w\leq u
\]
has background $(\varepsilon+\delta)\theta$. It supplies the asserted competitor. Apply \cref{lem:smaller-background-mass-lower} and let $\delta\downarrow0$ for the uniform estimate. The individual conclusion follows by taking any one such $\delta$. This is the lower-volume mechanism of \cite[Proposition 3.8]{ALS26}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:volume-monotonicity}
Let $\theta_1,\theta_2$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms on $X$. Suppose $\theta_1$ is big, $\theta_1\leq\theta_2$, and $u_i\in\PSH(X,\theta_i)$ satisfy $u_1\preceq u_2$. On a manifold with bounded mass,
\[
 \underline{\operatorname{vol}}_{\theta_1}(u_1)
 \leq\underline{\operatorname{vol}}_{\theta_2}(u_2),\qquad
 \overline{\operatorname{vol}}_{\theta_1}(u_1)
 \leq\overline{\operatorname{vol}}_{\theta_2}(u_2).
\]

\begin{proof}
We reconstruct \cite[Proposition 3.7]{BGL25} in the big regime. Shift $u_1$ so that $u_1\leq u_2$. Choose $v_2\simeq u_2$ in $\PSH(X,\theta_2)$ and, for real $t>0$, set
\[
 p_t=P_{\theta_1}(u_1+t,v_2).
\]
For $t>0$, a sufficiently low constant translate of $u_1$ is a competitor; also $p_t\leq u_1+t$. Thus $p_t\simeq u_1$. The contact theorem, applied in each background on the corresponding contact part, and positivity of the mixed products give
\[
 \mathrm{MA}_{\theta_1}(p_t)
 \leq\mathbf1_{\{u_1\leq v_2-t\}}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta_1}(u_1)
      +\mathrm{MA}_{\theta_2}(v_2).
\]
Indeed $p_t$ is also $\theta_2$-plurisubharmonic and is below $v_2$, so the contact inequality in that background applies. The first measure on the right has mass tending to zero: its indicators tend to zero off the pole sets, and the measure is finite and non-pluripolar. Integrate, let $t\to+\infty$, and then take the infimum over $v_2$.

\[

\begin{theorem}[Chiose]\label{thm:mass-invariance-characterization}
Let $\omega$ be a Hermitian form on a compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq2$. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\int_X(\omega+\ddc u)^n$ is independent of $u\in\HH_\omega$;
\item $\ddc(\omega^j)=0$ for $1\leq j\leq n-1$;
\item $\ddc\omega=0$ and $\mathrm{d}\omega\wedge\dc\omega=0$.
\end{enumerate}
They are also equivalent to constancy of the mass over all bounded $\omega$-plurisubharmonic functions. Consequently they characterize independence of $\mathcal V_\mu(\omega)$ from the smooth probability measure $\mu$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We give the polarization argument of \cite[Theorems~1--2]{Chiose16}. Assume the first condition. For every smooth real $u$, both signs of $tu$ are admissible when $|t|$ is small. The polynomial
$\int_X(\omega+t\ddc u)^n$ is therefore constant on an interval. Its nonconstant coefficients vanish. For $1\leq j\leq n-1$ this gives
\[
 \int_X\omega^j\wedge(\ddc u)^{n-j}=0.
\]
Replace $u$ by a linear combination of $n-j$ smooth real functions and compare the coefficient containing every parameter once. We obtain
\[
 \int_X\omega^j\wedge\ddc u_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\ddc u_{n-j}=0.
\]
Integration by parts in the first factor, followed by testing arbitrary $u_1$, yields the pointwise identity
\[
 \ddc(\omega^j)\wedge\ddc u_2\wedge\cdots\wedge\ddc u_{n-j}=0
\]
for every choice of the remaining functions. At a given point their complex Hessians can be prescribed arbitrarily: multiply a quadratic polynomial in a coordinate chart by a cutoff equal to one near that point. Complexifying the multilinear identity permits the quadratic monomials $z_a\bar z_b$. Products of their Hessians give all coordinate forms of complementary bidegree. Pairing with those forms shows that every coefficient of $\ddc(\omega^j)$ vanishes. When $j=n-1$, there are no remaining factors, and the same conclusion follows directly from testing $u_1$. This proves the second condition.

The variable-coefficient Evans--Krylov theorem \cite[Definition~3.2, Theorem~3.4, and the paragraph following it]{TWWY15} gives $u\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for some $0<\alpha<1$. The original equation is now uniformly elliptic with smooth data. Difference quotients satisfy linear equations whose principal coefficients are averages of inverse matrices along positive definite segments. Interior Schauder estimates first give $u\in C^{3,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and then, by iteration, $u\in C^\infty$. This proves (3)$\Rightarrow$(1). Finally, (1) and $F>0$ imply that the smooth semipositive matrix $T$ is positive definite, giving (2) and (3).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:unbounded-gauduchon-trace-density}
Let $u\in\PSH(X,\omega)$ and $0\leq g\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ satisfy
$\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega(u)\geq g\,\mathrm{d}V$. For every smooth Hermitian form $\gamma$,
\[
 (\omega+\ddc u)\wedge\gamma^{n-1}
       \geq(g\,\mathrm{d}V/\gamma^n)^{1/n}\gamma^n.
\]
The left side is the ordinary current paired with a smooth form; it retains any trace mass on the pole set of $u$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We first verify the bounded version with two different smooth backgrounds. Suppose $w\in\PSH(X,\omega)\cap L^\infty$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\omega(w)\geq q\,\mathrm{d}V$, where $0\leq q\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Put $\omega_w=\omega+\ddc w$. On a sufficiently small coordinate ball centered at $x$, let $\kappa$ be the Euclidean form and put $\beta=\omega(x)$, $\eta=\gamma(x)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, shrink the ball so that
\[
 \omega\leq\beta+\varepsilon\kappa\leq\omega+2\varepsilon\kappa,
 \qquad
 \gamma\leq\eta+\varepsilon\kappa\leq\gamma+2\varepsilon\kappa.
\]
Add to $w$ a quadratic potential of $\beta+\varepsilon\kappa$, and take a quadratic potential of $\eta+\varepsilon\kappa$. Both are bounded plurisubharmonic functions on the ball. Their top-degree measures dominate $q\,\mathrm{d}V$ and $\gamma^n$, respectively. The local mixed inequality used in \cref{lem:nonclosed-mixed-density}, namely \cite[Theorem 1.2]{Dinew09}, gives
\[
 (\omega_w+2\varepsilon\kappa)\wedge
             (\gamma+2\varepsilon\kappa)^{n-1}
 \geq(q\,\mathrm{d}V/\gamma^n)^{1/n}\gamma^n.
\]
For each $\varepsilon$ the small balls cover a fixed coordinate chart. The displayed measures depend polynomially on $\varepsilon$, with coefficients of locally finite variation. Let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ to obtain the bounded inequality.

destinations.paragraph: The local mixed inequality in \cref{thm:local-mixed-input} is \cite[Theorem 1.2]{Dinew09}, for locally bounded psh functions and nonnegative measurable smooth-volume densities. It supplies the local input in \cref{sec:interior-calculus}. Freezing the two smooth backgrounds gives \cref{lem:nonclosed-mixed-density} and the trace inequalities \eqref{eq:big-singular-gauduchon-trace} and \cref{lem:unbounded-gauduchon-trace-density}; the latter retains the linear trace mass on the pole set. The coefficient-freezing proof also recovers the smooth-volume inequality used in \cite[Lemma 1.9]{Nguyen16}.

Let $\mathrm{MA}_\omega(u)=\mathrm{MA}_\omega(v)=\mu=F\omega^n$, with
$F\in L^p$, $p>1$.  The mass identity gives $\mu(X)=V$.
If $u-v$ is nonconstant, shift $u$ so that its difference from $v$
has supremum $s>0$ and infimum $-s$.  Interchanging the pair if
necessary, arrange that $S=\{v<u\}$ satisfies $\mu(S)\leq V/2$.
Define
\[
 b_0=\frac{V-2\mu(S)}V\geq0,
 \qquad G=2F\mathbf1_S+b_0.
\]
This nonnegative $L^p$ function has total integral $V$, so choose the
continuous bounded solution $\rho$ of \eqref{uni-eq:aux-solvability}.
Take $C_0$ with $\rho-C_0\leq u$, and set
\[
 q_\delta=(1-\delta)u+\delta(\rho-C_0),\qquad
 E_\delta=\{v<q_\delta\}\subset S,
 \qquad 0<\delta<1.
\]
On $S$, the mixed inequality gives
\[
 \mathrm{MA}_\omega(q_\delta)\geq
 \bigl((1-\delta)+\delta2^{1/n}\bigr)^n\mu=:A_\delta\mu,
 \qquad A_\delta>1.
\]
Ordinary comparison on $E_\delta$ yields
\[
 A_\delta\mu(E_\delta)
 \leq\int_{E_\delta}\mathrm{MA}_\omega(q_\delta)
 \leq\int_{E_\delta}\mathrm{MA}_\omega(v)=\mu(E_\delta).
\]
Thus $\mu(E_\delta)=0$.  Bounded domination gives
$v\geq q_\delta$ everywhere; letting $\delta\downarrow0$ gives
$v\geq u$, contradicting $\sup_X(u-v)=s>0$.  Therefore the
difference is constant.  This is the restricted-density mass
concentration method of \cite[proof of Theorem~3.7 and Remark~3.8]{LPT20}, with its Hermitian comparison
interfaces made explicit.  It never divides by $F$, and permits $F$
to vanish on an open set.

records.paragraph:
The following exterior-ball proof follows the maximum-propagation method of \cite[Proposition~2.4 and Theorem~2.5 in the cited preprint]{BG18}. We give the argument for the present operator explicitly.  Let $W\in C^2$
satisfy $LW\geq0$ in a chart, suppose $W\leq M$, and put
$K=\{W=M\}$.  If $z\in K$ is a nearest point to $y\notin K$, then
\begin{equation}\label{uni-eq:normalzero}
 (y-z)^Ta(z)(y-z)=0.
\end{equation}
To prove this, suppose the left side is positive, set
$r_0=|y-z|$, and shrink the tangent ball toward $z$:
$y'=z+\theta(y-z)$, $R=\theta r_0$, with $0<\theta<1$ small.
The closed ball $\overline{B(y',R)}$ lies in the chart and meets $K$
only at $z$.  This follows from the triangle inequality; equality in
$|k-y|\leq|k-y'|+|y'-y|\leq r_0$, for $k\in K$, forces $k=z$.
For large $\gamma$, the function
\[
 \psi(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma R^2}-\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma|x-y'|^2}
\]
satisfies
\[
 L\psi=2\gamma \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma|x-y'|^2}
   \bigl(\operatorname{tr}a-2\gamma(x-y')^Ta(x)(x-y')\bigr)<0
\]
in a neighborhood of $z$.  Choose a sufficiently small $r<R$, and
consider the lens $D=B(z,r)\cap B(y',R)$.  On its boundary lying on the
outer tangent sphere, $\psi=0$ and $W-M\leq0$.  On the remaining
compact boundary portion, $W-M<0$, since the tangent ball meets $K$
only at $z$.  Hence, for sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$,
$W-M\leq\varepsilon\psi$ on $\partial D$.  A positive interior
maximum of $W-M-\varepsilon\psi$ would have nonpositive Hessian but
strictly positive image under $L$, which is impossible.  The same
inequality therefore holds in $D$.  Outside the tangent ball
$\psi\geq0$, so it also holds in a full neighborhood of $z$.
Second-order contact at $z$ now yields
\[
 0\leq LW(z)\leq\varepsilon L\psi(z)<0,
\]
proving \eqref{uni-eq:normalzero}.

destinations.paragraph: The exterior-ball proof leading to \eqref{uni-eq:normalzero} follows the maximum-propagation method of \cite[Proposition~2.4 and Theorem~2.5 in the cited preprint]{BG18}.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:lower-mass-trace-concentration}
For smooth real $(2,2)$-forms $\Theta$, the finite numbers
\[
 C_\delta=\sup\left\{\int_XB_\delta\wedge\Theta:
 \Theta>0,\ \ddc\Theta=0,\ \int_X\omega\wedge\Theta=1\right\},
\]
tend to infinity as $\delta\downarrow0$.
\end{lemma}
\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
\begin{proof}
For fixed $\delta$, choose a finite constant $M_\delta>0$ with $B_\delta\leq M_\delta\omega$. This inequality proves finiteness. Suppose instead that $C_{\delta_l}\leq C$ along a sequence tending to zero. Scaling the test forms and applying \cref{thm:lamari} to $C\omega-B_{\delta_l}$ gives normalized quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $v_l$ such that
\[
 C\omega+\ddc v_l\geq B_{\delta_l},\qquad \sup_Xv_l=0.
\]
By \cref{thm:normalized-compactness}, a subsequence converges in $L^1$ to a nontrivial $C\omega$-plurisubharmonic function $v$. The approximate identity in the $\zeta$ variable gives
\[
 B_{\delta_l}\rightharpoonup\chi[\zeta=0],\qquad
 C\omega+\ddc v\geq\chi[\zeta=0].
\]
On a coordinate ball where $\chi=1$, add a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function whose Hessian dominates $C\omega$. The resulting positive closed current dominates $[\zeta=0]$. Hence $v$ has Lelong number at least one on an open subset of this hypersurface. Smooth correction does not change Lelong numbers. Siu's analyticity theorem \cite[Main Theorem, p.~53]{Siu74} implies that
$Z=\{\nu(v,\cdot)\geq1\}$ is an analytic subset of $X$. It is proper because $v$ is not identically $-\infty$.

destinations.paragraph: The analyticity of positive Lelong level sets recalled in \cref{subsec:psh-lelong-levels} and used in \cref{lem:lower-mass-trace-concentration} is Siu's theorem \cite[Main Theorem, p.~53]{Siu74}. Smooth local corrections allow its application to quasi-plurisubharmonic functions.

For concentric coordinate balls $B'\Subset B$ and a Borel set $E\subset B'$, let $\operatorname{cap}(E,B)=\sup\{\int_E(\ddc v)^n:v\in\PSH(B),\ 0\leq v\leq1\}$ be the relative Bedford--Taylor capacity. We use two standard local estimates on these balls, with constants $C,a>0$ depending only on the nested balls and the fixed volume form:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $w\leq0$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$ and $v$ is bounded and plurisubharmonic, then
\[
 \int_{B'}|w|(\ddc v)^n
 \leq C\|w\|_{L^1(B)}\|v\|_{L^\infty(B)}^n.
\]
An additive constant can first be chosen in $v$. This is the weighted Chern--Levine--Nirenberg inequality.
\item For every Borel set $E\subset B'$, the relative Bedford--Taylor capacity satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{Vol}(E)\leq C\exp\bigl(-a\operatorname{cap}(E,B)^{-1/n}\bigr),
\]
with value zero when the capacity is zero. This is the classical local volume--capacity estimate.
\end{enumerate}
These are statements of local pluripotential theory, as developed in \cite[Chapters 3 and 4]{GZ17}; the bounded product and capacity conventions also agree, up to harmless fixed constants, with \cite[Chapter 2]{SGPT}. We will not import a global Hermitian capacity estimate. The deductions below recover the estimates used in \cite[Section 5]{KN15} and \cite[Section 6]{Dinew16}.

destinations.paragraph: The local capacity deductions used for the weak equations recover the estimates of \cite[Section 5]{KN15} and \cite[Section 6]{Dinew16}. Their inputs are local pluripotential estimates, rather than an assumed global Hermitian capacity bound.
